questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: Why does Mara walk through the garden?

choices.A: To observe details that could improve the sign
choices.B: To ask visitors what the sign should say
choices.C: To find a different board for the sign
choices.D: To decide where the committee should plant flowers

questions.correctAnswer: To observe details that could improve the sign
questions.explanation: Mara studies the garden's vines, leaves, and angles before revising the sign's design.
questions.stimulusText:
Mara had promised the neighborhood garden committee that its new wooden sign would be ready by Saturday. On Friday afternoon, however, the painted letters looked stiff and uneven. She had copied them carefully from a computer printout, yet the sign seemed more suited to an office hallway than to a garden filled with curling vines and bright zinnias.
Her grandfather found her sanding away a blot of green paint. “The letters are readable,” he said.
“Readable is not the same as welcoming,” Mara replied.
Instead of starting over, she walked through the garden. She noticed how bean tendrils looped around their poles and how sunflower leaves leaned at different angles. Back in the shed, she softened the straight edges of the letters and added small painted leaves between the words. One leaf tilted too far, and a drop of yellow landed beneath it. Mara nearly wiped it away. Then she turned the drop into a tiny bee.
The next morning, visitors paused at the gate to admire the sign. A child pointed first to the bee, not the words. Mara smiled. The mistake she had almost erased had given the sign the lively quality she had been seeking.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: According to the passage, why might a borrower be required to attend a lesson?

choices.A: To learn how to use specialized equipment safely
choices.B: To qualify for a lower yearly membership fee
choices.C: To help inspect every object in the collection
choices.D: To teach another member a repair skill

questions.correctAnswer: To learn how to use specialized equipment safely
questions.explanation: The passage states that some borrowers must complete a safety lesson before using specialized equipment.
questions.stimulusText:
At a traditional library, members borrow books. At a “library of things,” they may borrow a drill, a telescope, a sewing machine, or a set of camping pans. These lending programs have appeared in many communities because people often need certain objects only briefly. Buying each item can be expensive, and storing rarely used equipment takes space.
The system resembles ordinary library lending. Members reserve an item, collect it for a stated period, and return it so another person can use it. Some programs charge a yearly fee, while others are supported by donations or local funding. Before borrowing specialized equipment, members may have to attend a short safety lesson.
The benefits extend beyond saving money. Sharing objects can reduce the number of products manufactured and later discarded. The programs may also encourage neighbors to exchange knowledge. A person borrowing a sewing machine, for example, might attend a repair workshop taught by an experienced volunteer.
Running such a library requires careful planning. Tools must be inspected, missing parts replaced, and popular objects scheduled fairly. Yet supporters argue that these challenges are manageable. To them, a shelf holding one well-used tool is more valuable than many closets each holding an identical tool that is almost never touched.

questions.skill: Main Idea, Central Thought, or Summary
questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?

choices.A: Sustained observation can deepen understanding in museums and everyday life.
choices.B: Museum labels prevent viewers from forming independent opinions.
choices.C: People need expert training to interpret unfamiliar paintings.
choices.D: Quick decisions are usually less accurate than slow decisions.

questions.correctAnswer: Sustained observation can deepen understanding in museums and everyday life.
questions.explanation: The passage argues that slow, careful attention reveals details and patterns across many settings.
questions.stimulusTitle: The Value of a Slow Look
questions.stimulusText:
In a museum, visitors sometimes move from painting to painting as though they are collecting proof that they saw each one. A quick glance may reveal a subject, a dominant color, or a familiar name. It rarely reveals how the parts of a work guide the eye or how a small detail changes the mood.
Looking slowly does not require expert knowledge. A viewer can begin with simple questions: Where did my eyes land first? Which line or color led them elsewhere? What detail did I miss at first? These questions shift attention from identifying the picture to experiencing how it works.
Slow looking can also make uncertainty useful. A puzzling expression on a painted face may invite several explanations. Rather than rushing to read the museum label, a viewer can gather evidence from posture, setting, and light. The label may later provide context, but it need not replace observation.
This habit matters beyond museums. Careful attention helps people notice assumptions in advertisements, patterns in scientific observations, and changes in familiar places. Speed is valuable when a decision must be made quickly. Yet when understanding matters more than coverage, giving one object sustained attention can reveal more than hurrying past twenty.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What problem does Ms. Alvarez discover?

choices.A: A pad beneath one of Jonah's clarinet keys is torn.
choices.B: Jonah has practiced the wrong opening melody.
choices.C: The orchestra cabinet has no spare instruments.
choices.D: Priya's violin needs a new string.

questions.correctAnswer: A pad beneath one of Jonah's clarinet keys is torn.
questions.explanation: Ms. Alvarez examines the clarinet and finds a torn pad beneath one key.
questions.stimulusText:
For weeks, Jonah had practiced the opening melody for the school orchestra concert. During the final rehearsal, however, his clarinet produced a thin squeak on the third note. He tried again, with the same result. Around him, chairs scraped as the other musicians settled into place.
Ms. Alvarez examined the instrument and discovered a torn pad beneath one key. There was no time to replace it before rehearsal began. “You can use the spare clarinet,” she said, handing Jonah an older instrument from the cabinet.
The spare felt unfamiliar. Its keys resisted his fingers, and its tone seemed darker than the one he knew. Jonah wanted to ask someone else to play the opening. Instead, he took a slow breath and tested the difficult measures quietly. By the third attempt, his hands had adjusted.
When Ms. Alvarez raised her baton, Jonah began. The first phrase was not as polished as it had sounded at home, but it was steady. Later, during a rest, he noticed that Priya, the new violinist, was staring anxiously at her music. Jonah caught her eye and nodded toward the conductor. Priya straightened and lifted her bow.
After rehearsal, Jonah returned the spare clarinet. He had not played perfectly, yet the instrument no longer felt like an obstacle. It had become proof that preparation could include adapting when a plan changed.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What causes collected droplets to move from the mesh into the channel?

choices.A: Heat
choices.B: Gravity
choices.C: A fuel-powered pump
choices.D: A protective coating

questions.correctAnswer: Gravity
questions.explanation: The passage states that gravity pulls drops heavy enough to move into the channel.
questions.stimulusText:
In some dry coastal regions, rain is scarce even though thick fog frequently moves across hillsides. Fog collectors can capture some of the water carried in that air. A typical collector consists of a fine mesh panel held upright by a frame. As wind pushes fog through the mesh, tiny droplets strike the threads and join together. Once the drops become heavy enough, gravity pulls them into a channel below the panel. From there, the water flows into a storage container.
The amount collected depends on several factors. A site needs regular fog and enough wind to move moist air through the mesh. The threads must be spaced closely enough to catch droplets but not so closely that they block airflow. Researchers also test different materials and coatings to help drops slide downward rather than remain on the panel.
Fog collectors do not create water, and they cannot supply every community with all the water it needs. Their usefulness varies by location and season. Still, they can provide water for gardens, tree seedlings, or other limited purposes where suitable conditions exist. Because the panels require no fuel to operate, they may serve as a simple addition to other water sources. Careful site testing remains essential: a collector placed where fog is rare may gather almost nothing, no matter how well the mesh is designed.

questions.stimulusText:
Before electronic communication reached many mountain communities, sending an urgent message could require a rider to travel for hours. In one region, a group of towns created a chain of signal stations on high ridges. The system described here is a historical-style example rather than a record of one specific network.
Each station could see the station before it and the one after it. Operators used pairs of movable wooden arms mounted on a tall post. Different arm positions represented letters, numbers, or short instructions. An operator viewed an incoming signal through a telescope, recorded it, and then repeated it for the next station. In clear weather, a message could cross the region far faster than a horse could carry it.
Speed did not guarantee accuracy. A tired operator might copy an angle incorrectly, and mist could hide a station entirely. To reduce mistakes, operators paused after a group of symbols and waited for a confirmation signal. Important messages were also written in a log so that the sequence could be checked later.
The network required trained workers and unobstructed views, which made it expensive to maintain. Eventually, telegraph wires offered a more dependable way to send messages in poor visibility and after dark. Even so, the ridge stations demonstrated an important principle: information can travel quickly when a long journey is divided among connected points.

choices.C: Reeds were caught around the rudder.
choices.D: Eli had placed the boat facing the wrong way.

questions.explanation: Mara finds the off-center metal weight after the boat circles.
questions.stimulusText:
Mara had tested her model boat three times in the bathtub, but the park pond looked far less forgiving. A breeze wrinkled the water, and reeds leaned over the launch spot. She set the cedar boat down. It traveled barely a yard before turning in a slow circle.
“The sail is crooked,” her cousin Eli said.
Mara wanted to blame the wind. Instead, she pulled the boat ashore and examined the mast. The sail was straight, but the small metal weight beneath the hull had shifted to one side. She remembered fastening it hurriedly after dinner.
Using a coin as a screwdriver, Mara loosened the weight and centered it. The second launch began badly too: a gust pushed the boat toward the reeds. Then the sail caught steady air, and the boat moved across the pond in a clean diagonal line.
Eli ran along the bank, cheering. Mara stayed near the launch spot, watching the wake narrow behind the boat. She had imagined success as proof that her design was perfect. Instead, the best moment had come from discovering exactly where it was not. She opened her notebook and wrote, “Test outdoors earlier.” Below that she added, “Bring a real screwdriver.”

questions.stimulusText:
On Saturday morning, Luis stood inside the neighborhood museum holding a stack of blank labels. His job was to place them beside objects in a new exhibit about everyday inventions. The curator had arranged an early alarm clock, a folding ruler, and a hand-cranked eggbeater in glass cases.
Luis began copying descriptions from a folder. At the eggbeater, he paused. The description explained its gears but not why anyone had valued it. He pictured visitors glancing at the object and moving on.
In a storage box, Luis found a note donated with the eggbeater. Its owner recalled using it every Sunday while her brother slowly poured batter into a bowl. Luis asked the curator whether he could add one sentence from the memory. She read the note, then nodded.
When the museum doors opened, a family stopped at the case. A boy turned the handle of an identical eggbeater mounted outside the glass. His grandfather pointed to the label and described making pancakes without an electric mixer. Luis watched them talk until the next visitors arrived.
He had thought labels simply named and explained things. Now he understood that a few careful words could also open a door between an object and someone’s own experience.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why are young trees planted close together?

choices.A: Competition for light encourages upward growth.
choices.B: Close planting eliminates the need for watering.
choices.C: Dense roots prevent leaves from reaching the soil.
choices.D: Crowded trees remain shorter than park trees.

questions.correctAnswer: Competition for light encourages upward growth.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly connects close planting with rapid upward growth.
questions.stimulusText:
Some cities are creating dense patches of native trees on plots no larger than a tennis court. These “tiny forests” differ from ordinary parks. Instead of spacing a few mature trees across open lawns, planners place many young trees and shrubs close together. The plants compete for sunlight, encouraging rapid upward growth, while fallen leaves remain on the ground and enrich the soil.
Before planting, teams study nearby natural woodlands to identify native species. They may loosen compacted soil and mix in compost so roots can spread. Volunteers then plant several layers of vegetation, including low shrubs, medium-height trees, and species that may eventually form a canopy.
Tiny forests cannot replace large natural forests. Their small size limits the wildlife they can support, and young plantings require watering and weeding. However, they can cool a neighborhood, absorb rainwater, provide habitat for insects and birds, and give residents a nearby place to observe seasonal change.
Researchers continue to measure how well these forests perform in different climates. The most useful comparisons follow planted sites for years and compare them with similar unplanted areas. Such studies can help cities decide where dense planting offers the greatest benefit and where another use of limited land would serve residents better.

questions.stimulusText:
Nia had practiced the drum pattern until her hands knew it without help. Yet during rehearsal, the dancers repeatedly reached the stage's center one beat after her final strike. Mr. Chen asked everyone to begin again. Nia played louder, certain that a stronger rhythm would solve the problem. The dancers still arrived late.
During the break, Nia sat at the edge of the stage and tapped the pattern against her knee. Across the room, Mateo silently practiced the dancers' opening steps. Nia noticed that he paused before the third turn to avoid a loose strip of tape on the floor. Each dancer made the same tiny adjustment.
Nia peeled up the tape and asked Mateo to try the steps again. Without the obstacle, he reached center exactly on her final tap. When rehearsal resumed, the whole group landed together.
“Good catch,” Mr. Chen said.
Nia looked at her drum. She had assumed that any timing problem belonged to the musician. Playing louder had only made the mismatch easier to hear. The solution had come when she watched what the rhythm was guiding.

Mr. Chen asked everyone to begin again. Nia played louder, certain that a stronger rhythm would solve the problem. The dancers still arrived late.
During the break, Nia sat at the edge of the stage and tapped the pattern against her knee. Across the room, Mateo silently practiced the dancers' opening steps. Nia noticed that he paused before the third turn to avoid a loose strip of tape on the floor. Each dancer made the same tiny adjustment.
Nia peeled up the tape and asked Mateo to try the steps again. Without the obstacle, he reached center exactly on her final tap. When rehearsal resumed, the whole group landed together.
“Good catch,” Mr. Chen said.
Nia looked at her drum. She had assumed that any timing problem belonged to the musician. Playing louder had only made the mismatch easier to hear. The solution had come when she watched what the rhythm was guiding.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does sandy soil drain quickly?

choices.A: Its particles contain large spaces between them.
choices.B: Its organic matter blocks water near the surface.
choices.C: Its earthworms remove moisture from plant roots.
choices.D: Its particles absorb more water than clay does.

questions.correctAnswer: Its particles contain large spaces between them.
questions.explanation: The passage says water passes quickly through the relatively large spaces in sandy soil.
questions.stimulusText:
After a heavy rain, water does not move through every soil at the same speed. The size of the spaces between soil particles helps determine what happens. Sandy soil contains relatively large spaces. Water can pass through them quickly, so sand drains well but may not hold moisture near plant roots for long. Clay soil has much smaller spaces. It often absorbs water slowly and can remain wet after rain.
Organic matter, such as decomposed leaves, changes this picture. Mixed into sandy soil, it acts somewhat like a sponge, holding water that might otherwise drain away. In dense clay, organic matter helps create larger pathways through which water and air can travel.
Earthworms also influence these underground routes. As they tunnel, they form channels that allow water to enter soil rather than flowing across its surface. Their castings add nutrients and contribute organic material.
Gardeners cannot easily replace all the soil in a yard, but they can improve how it handles water. Adding compost, avoiding repeated walking on damp ground, and keeping living roots in the soil can protect the spaces water needs. Healthy soil is not merely a pile of particles; it is a changing network of passages.

choices.B: To move student stakes closer to the water
choices.C: To check unusual results that images or software may produce
choices.D: To replace surface models with handwritten maps

questions.correctAnswer: To check unusual results that images or software may produce
questions.explanation: The passage states that plants, shadows, and waves can affect aerial results, so Ortiz checks them in person.
questions.stimulusText:
When coastal surveyor Lena Ortiz began her career, measuring a beach meant carrying poles, notebooks, and a heavy leveling instrument across the sand. Her team returned to the same marked locations each season. By comparing the height and position of the shoreline over time, they could tell where storms had removed sand and where currents had deposited it.
Years later, Ortiz began using small camera-equipped aircraft to record the coast from above. Software combined hundreds of images into detailed surface models. The new method covered more ground and revealed patterns that isolated measurements could miss. It did not, however, make fieldwork unnecessary. Plants could hide the sand, shadows could confuse the software, and waves could erase a temporary marker. Ortiz still walked the beach to check unusual results.
She also invited local students to place simple measuring stakes beyond the reach of ordinary tides. Their monthly photographs created a steady record between the team's larger surveys. Ortiz valued the project not only for its data but also for the questions students began asking about dunes, storms, and building near the shore.
For Ortiz, better instruments did more than increase speed. They made it possible to connect precise measurements, direct observation, and community attention to a coastline that never remained still.
